title: DOAH 26-0122 Recommended Order: LUTHER SAUNDERS vs. MIAMI-DADE COUNTY
text:
STATE OF FLORIDA
DIVISION OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
LUTHER SAUNDERS,
Petitioner,
vs. Case No. 26-0122
MIAMI-DADE COUNTY,
Respondent.
/
RECOMMENDED ORDER
A hearing was conducted in this proceeding by Zoom conference on
April 13 and 22, 2026, before Administrative Law Judge Robert Kilbride of
the Division of Administrative Hearings ("DOAH").
APPEARANCES
For Petitioner: Leslie Phyllis Holland, Esquire
Law Office of Leslie Holland
Post Office Box 600637
North Miami Beach, Florida 33160
For Respondent: Zachary Vosseler, Esquire
Miami-Dade County Attorney's Office
111 Northwest First Street, Suite 2810
Miami, Florida 33128
STATEMENT OF THE ISSUE
Whether Petitioner proved that Respondent engaged in unlawful
retaliation against Petitioner at his place of employment, in violation of
section 760.10, Florida Statutes (2023), as alleged.1
1 The 2022 version of chapter 760, which was in effect at the time of the most recent alleged
discriminatory conduct, applies to this proceeding.

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT
On June 3, 2025, Petitioner, Luther Saunders ("Petitioner" or "Saunders"),
filed an Employment Complaint of Discrimination with the Florida
Commission on Human Relations ("FCHR") alleging that Respondent,
Miami-Dade County ("Respondent" or the "County"), Department of Transit
and Public Works ("DTPW") had engaged in unlawful retaliation against him.
Following an investigation of the alleged discriminatory conduct, on
November 25, 2025, FCHR issued a Determination: No Reasonable Cause,
concluding that it was unlikely that unlawful discrimination occurred.
Pursuant to the Notice of Determination: No Reasonable Cause, Saunders
filed a Petition for Relief on December 28, 2025, reiterating his allegations of
unlawful work retaliation and requesting an administrative hearing
pursuant to sections 120.569 and 120.57(1), Florida Statutes.
This matter was referred to DOAH for assignment to an administrative
law judge to conduct a final hearing on the complaint of discrimination, and
his subsequent petition. The final hearing was conducted over two days, on
April 13 and 22, 2026.
Saunders testified on his own behalf and presented the testimony from
current or former DTPW employees, Ronessa Wilson, Manny Fresnedo, and
James Graham. Both parties presented the testimony of Lead Transit
Operations Supervisor ("TOS") Carlos Robledo.
The County presented testimony of then–Acting Section Chief Elena
Najarro; Lead TOSs Lakeisha Terrell, Rene Molina, Cedric Dallas; TOS and
Union Representative Ernest Charles; TOS Andrew Allen; Superintendent
Omar Yoda; General Superintendent Schneider St. Preux; DTPW Office of
2

Civil Rights and Labor Relations Manager Cindy LaBranche; and Deputy
Director Sean Adgerson. Petitioner's Composite Exhibits A, B, C, and D were
admitted into evidence. Respondent's Exhibits 1, 2, and 3 were also admitted
into evidence.
The three-volume Transcript of the final hearing was filed on May 15,
2026. Proposed recommended orders for both parties were filed, reviewed,
and considered before preparing this Recommended Order.
References to statutes, rules, or policies refer to those in effect on the date
of the action, omission, or occurrence. Exhibits are referred to as "Pet. Ex."
and "Resp. Ex.," followed by the exhibit number and page, where applicable.
FINDINGS OF FACT
The undersigned makes the following findings of material and relevant
facts:
Saunders's Work Background
1. Saunders worked as a bus operator for the County beginning December
2014, and served as an out-of-class instructor for new bus operator trainees,
from August 2022 to November 2023.
2. In November 2023, Saunders was promoted to TOS and served a
12-month probationary period under Superintendent Omar Yoda.
3. Following his promotion, Saunders completed an initial training
program of approximately four months under the instruction of Lead TOSs
Rene Molina and Cedric Dallas, among others.
The TOS Position and Probationary Process
4. Under the County Personnel Rules for the Classified Service,
Chapter III, Section 11, the probationary period is an integral and necessary
part of the examination process for promoted employees. Probation is
3

designed to closely observe an employee's work and provides the option to fail
an employee whose performance does not meet the required standards.
5. Significantly, a department head or authorized designee may remove or
demote a probationary employee at any time prior to the expiration of the
probationary period, without charges and without the right of appeal.
6. A probationary TOS employee who fails probation is demoted and
returns to the position he/she held prior to promotion. Resp. Ex. 1, at 4 and 5.
7. A TOS performs two broad categories of duties. First, a TOS working an
indoor assignment operates from a dispatch window at a bus garage, where
the TOS may assign work to bus operators, manages bus availability, assigns
buses to departing operators, handles schedule adjustments in real time, and
tracks on-time performance. This role requires multitasking simultaneous
and pressing demands within short timeframes.
8. Second, a TOS works road assignment patrol zones in a County car,
where he/she may respond to accidents and incidents, communicates with
central control, and manages terminals.
9. The process for failing a probationary TOS employee at DTPW requires
the superintendent to prepare a memorandum documenting performance
concerns and attaching supporting documentation, followed by concurrences
from several supervisory/management personnel, including the section chief,
general superintendent, assistant director, as well as a review by the Office of
Civil Rights and Labor Relations. Ultimately, the deputy director makes the
final decision.
The Meeting of March 29, 2024
10. During Saunders's period of training, supervisors informally
communicated concerns to Yoda about complaints being raised by Saunders
regarding the difficulty of his new job responsibilities and the supervision he
was receiving.
4

11. Four witnesses–Yoda, Acting Section Chief Elena Najarro, Molina,
and Dallas–each independently documented and testified that they attended
a meeting with Saunders on or around March 29, 2024.
12. Their accounts varied a bit, but were consistent in most material
respects. They related that a meeting was held at the Coral Way Division; it
was convened by Yoda with Najarro, Molina, and Dallas in attendance. The
purpose of the meeting was to communicate performance expectations to
Saunders, offer him resources and support, and provide Saunders an
opportunity to voice concerns.
13. At the meeting, Saunders expressed that the job involved too many
tasks at once and stated that management did not know what it was doing.
When he was offered additional training, he responded that he considered
more training to be punishment and would rather return to his bus operator
position.
14. Najarro's email memorializing the meeting is dated May 14, 2024;
Molina's is dated May 15, 2024; Dallas's is dated May 16, 2024; and Yoda's
memorandum summarizing the same meeting is dated May 20, 2024. See
Resp. Ex. 1, at 4-8. Najarro and Molina referenced the March 29, 2024, date
in emails written before Yoda's memorandum was prepared suggesting that
they independently recalled the date of the meeting.
15. Saunders denied that a meeting involving himself, Yoda, Najarro,
Molina, and Dallas occurred on March 29, 2024. He testified that whatever
meeting he recalled, occurred in February 2024, before his probation began,
lasted approximately 45 minutes, and concerned his request for additional
training. He asserted that the March 29, 2024, date reflected in the
supporting documentation from these witnesses is simply wrong.
16. The undersigned determines that meeting involving Saunders, Yoda,
Najarro, Molina, and Dallas occurred on or around March 29, 2024, and that
the substance and nature of the meeting was as described by Respondent's
witnesses. Saunders's denial–standing alone against four independently
5

corroborating accounts memorialized in writing by different authors–is not
credited.
17. In any event, even accepting Saunders's own account that the meeting
took place on a different day, a multi-attendee meeting did occur during
which Saunders expressed frustration with the TOS position, management
communicated performance expectations, and an offer of additional training
was extended.
Saunders's Performance Problems Continue
18. Saunders's first independent dispatch assignment began April 8, 2024,
approximately three weeks into his probation. He was assigned to the
Northeast Division on a 12:00 p.m. to 8:00 p.m. shift. This was his first time
working independently as a dispatcher without a trainer present.
19. Lead TOS Carlos Robledo, who worked the adjacent dispatch window
around this time, testified that he had to intervene to assist Saunders on
multiple occasions. Robledo observed that Saunders had difficulty assigning
buses to operators who had checked in on time, resulting in buses leaving
late. Robledo also assisted with splitting assignments.
20. Robledo acknowledged that three other probationary TOS employees
working at or around the same time, required similar interventions; however,
all passed probation. He clarified that Saunders "probably had the most
errors" compared to the other three.
21. Lead TOS Lakeisha Terrell sent Yoda an email on April 17, 2024,
documenting her observations of Saunders's dispatch performance on April 8
and 10, 2024.
22. Terrell wrote that Saunders failed to dispatch and assign available
bus operators, causing several routes not to go out on time and requiring
splits due to dispatch errors. She recounted that he repeatedly failed to
employ strategies and skills already covered in training and that he failed to
take command of issues that arose.
6

23. Instead Saunders made excuses to her, stating "I can't multitask,"
"Management can't even do this job. All they do is sit upstairs. I am not
experienced, and they should have someone else doing this."
24. Notably, she further wrote that, when he was asked whether he
needed additional training, Saunders stated he would rather go back to the
bus (bus operator work), and instructed her to call Yoda stating, "Yes, send
me back because this is too much." Resp. Ex. 1, at 10.
25. Saunders denied making any of the statements attributed to him in
Terrell's email.
26. The undersigned credits Terrell's account of Saunders's activity on
two separate days. Her email was written shortly after the events occurred,
and Saunders offers no basis for finding she had a motive to fabricate these
statements. Saunders's denial is not credited and is rejected.
April 18, 2024, Phone Call and Meeting
27. After receiving Terrell's email documenting Saunders's dispatch
deficiencies, Yoda decided to meet with him to address those concerns. Before
Yoda had the chance to do so, Saunders called Yoda by telephone on the
morning of April 18, 2024.
28. Yoda testified that Saunders was screaming on the phone, to the point
where he had to hold the phone away from his ear, and instructed Saunders
to lower his voice before the conversation could continue. Yoda decided he
needed to drive to the Northeast Division to meet with Saunders in person.
29. Saunders testified that during this phone call, he told Yoda that he
(Yoda) had a history of treating black employees poorly, referencing what he
knew of the situations involving two other black employees, James Graham
and Javon Ferguson. Yoda "did not recall" those comments being made by
Saunders.
7

30. After arriving at the Northeast Division facility, Yoda waited
approximately 30 minutes while Saunders was on his phone attempting to
get in touch with his union president or other union official, ostensibly to
have them participate in the meeting with him. Lead TOS Terrell was
present, as well.
31. When Saunders joined them, the meeting became contentious.
Saunders was loud, combative, and resistant to the performance feedback
Yoda was attempting to provide him. Saunders made statements to the effect
that the job was impossible and that management did not know what it was
doing. Resp. Ex. 1, at 4 and 5.
32. Ernest Charles, the union representative, eventually arrived, but the
meeting was already under way. He could hear loud voices from outside the
closed office door and he had to knock twice before being admitted.
33. Upon entering the room, Charles observed a heated exchange between
Saunders and Yoda. Charles asked Saunders to step outside so that Charles
could speak privately with Yoda and Terrell.
34. Yoda told Charles, in substance, that he needed to deal with this
situation now. Charles testified that he did not hear Yoda use words to the
effect–"He'll be untouchable" after probation is over. Charles's denial of
hearing the word "untouchable" is credited.
35. At one point during the meeting, Saunders rubbed the skin of his arm
and said to Yoda, "I know what this is about." Yoda understood this gesture
and statement to mean that Saunders was accusing him of racial
discrimination.
36. Terrell and Charles testified that they both observed the arm-rubbing
gesture. Terrell testified that she understood the gesture the same way as
Yoda. Yoda did not respond to the gesture.
37. Following the meeting, Terrell sent a second email to Yoda on April 18,
2024, at 5:30 p.m., documenting that during the 4:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. lot
manager shift, Saunders had difficulty keeping up with bus and manpower
8

assignments, that Robledo had to intervene on several occasions by assisting
him with assigning operators, that Saunders failed to assign buses that were
available on the garage dashboard, and that Saunders had issues splitting up
assignments for personnel. Resp. Ex. 1, at 9.
38. Yoda testified that, taken together with the April 17, 2024, email and
the conduct during the phone call and meeting, he concluded that Saunders's
probation should be failed based on his documented performance failures and
the insubordinate conduct during the call and meeting. His decision, he said,
was not based on the skin-rubbing gesture or because Saunders made any
complaints of race discrimination. This evidence is credited.
Manual Fresnedo's Account
39. Bus Traffic Controller Manuel Fresnedo testified that sometime in
April 2024, Yoda approached him in the bus traffic control center and asked
how Saunders was performing in his street supervisor role.
40. Upon hearing a positive report from him, Yoda remarked that he was
not going to pass Saunders's probation, that he did not care who his cousin
was, and used profanity to express a personal dislike for Saunders, stating he
did not like his "fucking ass."
41. Fresnedo submitted an affidavit to the FCHR in August 2025,
documenting a version of this conversation. Neither document referenced
Yoda using the phrase "black ass," a phrase Fresnedo used for the first time
during the hearing.
42. Yoda denied ever speaking with Fresnedo about Saunders in any
context and testified he would never speak to a subordinate in the manner
Fresnedo described. Tr. 354.
43. Cindy LaBranche, a manager with DTPW's Office of Civil Rights and
Labor Relations, testified that during her internal investigation into
Saunders' complaint, she spoke with Fresnedo, who reported that Yoda had
made some type of derogatory, profanity-laden statement about Saunders.
9

44. LaBranche followed up but ultimately could not corroborate that the
conversation between Fresnedo and Yoda occurred. She identified a potential
source of bias: at the time of her investigation, there was a separate, pending
complaint filed by Fresnedo against Yoda.
45. Fresnedo's account of Yoda's statements is given limited weight, but
ultimately does not have a bearing on the outcome of this case.
46. Fresnedo acknowledged on cross-examination that Yoda said
nothing to him about retaliating against Saunders for complaining about
discrimination, nothing about the skin-rubbing gesture or any protected
activity, is significant.
47. Regardless, uncivil or profane comments by a supervisor, standing
alone, are not determinative regarding the issue of retaliation. When weighed
against the other overwhelming evidence of poor job performance, refusal to
embrace the duties of the new position, and his insubordinate behavior–these
off-hand comments pale in comparison.
48. Saunders testified to two instances of exemplary performance during
his probationary period: dispatching a bus operator for a reasonable-
suspicion alcohol and drug test in late April 2024 (the operator tested
positive), and assisting at a three-car accident scene on May 19, 2024, using
his fire extinguisher. Saunders testified he emailed supervisors about both
events and received no response. Neither email was placed in evidence.
49. These events, while commendable, do not contradict the documented
record of numerous dispatch and lot manager performance deficiencies.
Andrew Allen and Other Probationary TOS Employees
50. Andrew Allen is a black male who was in the same TOS training class
as Saunders and began his probationary period at the same time. He was
supervised by Yoda. Allen successfully completed his probationary period and
remained a TOS at the time of the hearing.
10

51. Allen testified that Yoda was a fair manager and a "stand-up guy" who
expected employees to do their jobs without excuses. Significantly, Allen
observed no racial bias by Yoda and testified that race never came up in their
interactions.
52. Allen stated he never told any supervisor the TOS job was too much,
never expressed a desire to return to his bus operator position, and was never
treated differently by Yoda because of his race.
53. Nashay Roberts and Woods were also probationary TOS employees
supervised by Yoda around the time of Saunders's probation. Both are black
and successfully passed their probationary periods.
54. In sum, during Saunders's probationary period, Yoda oversaw four
probationary TOS employees: Saunders, Allen, Roberts, and Woods. Three
passed probation. All three who passed are black. Only Saunders did not
pass.
The James Graham Evidence
55. The testimony of James Graham was admitted for the purpose of
assessing the objective reasonableness of Saunders's belief that he was being
subjected to racial discrimination.
56. Graham is a black male who testified that he was a probationary bus
traffic controller under Yoda's supervision from approximately July 2021 to
July 2022.
57. Yoda recommended failing his probation approximately two weeks
before its end date, in July 2022. Graham testified that Ferguson, also a
black bus traffic controller in the same class, had his probation failed at the
same time, while a Hispanic classmate passed.
58. Graham filed an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission
("EEOC") charge of discrimination in April 2023. That charge resulted in no
finding of discrimination.
11

59. Graham testified that Yoda called him "lazy," banged his fist on the
desk, used profanity in addressing him, and was intimidating. Graham did
not characterize these behaviors as involving explicit racial language.
60. He acknowledged on cross-examination that Yoda never explicitly
referenced his race, that the word "lazy" could be directed at any employee
regardless of race, and that his EEOC charge produced no finding of
discrimination.
61. Graham's testimony was given limited weight because it was more
than two years before the conduct in question. Also, uncivil or profane
comment alone do not prove retaliation, racial bias, or discrimination.
62. Saunders's knowledge of Graham and Ferguson, their complaints, and
their relation and interaction with Yoda as probationary employees were
noted.
The Failure-of-Protection Recommendation and Review Process
63. Yoda prepared a two-page memorandum dated May 20, 2024, to James
Rowan, chief of the DTPW Office of Civil Rights and Labor Relations. In it, he
requested that Saunders's probationary status be failed.
64. The memorandum is extensive and described the March 29, 2024,
meeting, the pattern of performance deficiencies, the April 17 and 18 events,
and Saunders's stated desire to return to his bus operator position. Attached
to the memorandum were Terrell's April 17 and 18 emails, Najarro's May 14
email, Molina's May 15 email, and Dallas's May 16 email. Resp. Ex. 1, at
4-10.
65. Yoda's memorandum also described Saunders's skin-rubbing gesture
and the ensuing confrontation at the April 18, 2024, meeting as part of his
account of that day's events.
66. Yoda testified his inclusion of the skin-rubbing incident was simply his
account of what occurred and did not form the basis for his recommendation.
Rather, his request to fail Saunders's probation rested on the documented
12

performance record and Saunders's insubordinate conduct during the phone
call and meeting.
67. Najarro reviewed the package and concurred on May 22, 2024, that
failure of Saunders's probation was appropriate. Her concurrence was based
on her independent review of the documentation and her firsthand
observations of Saunders at the March 29, 2024, meeting. Najarro also
testified she was unaware of any complaint of race discrimination by
Saunders at the time she concurred.
68. General Superintendent Schneider St. Preux also reviewed the
package and concurred. He was informed by Yoda by phone shortly after the
April 18, 2024, meeting of the skin-rubbing incident. He also separately
spoke with Terrell, who corroborated the account.
69. St. Preux testified that the skin-rubbing gesture was surprising but
played no role in his concurrence. Rather, it was based solely on the
documented record of Saunders's poor performance.
70. Assistant Director Joel Perez reviewed and concurred in the
recommendation as well.
71. The Office of Civil Rights and Labor Relations reviewed the package
and found that management followed applicable policies and procedures and
that the supporting documentation was sufficient to proceed.
72. LaBranche testified that the process in Saunders's case was consistent
with standard practice and that she was unable to corroborate his retaliation
allegations in her investigation.
73. Deputy Director Sean Adgerson reviewed the complete failure-of-
probation package, including the memorandum, all attached emails, and the
concurrences of Najarro, St. Preux, Perez, and the Office of Civil Rights and
Labor Relations.
74. Adgerson testified that his decision was based on two factors: (1) the
documented evidence that Saunders was struggling with the work and had
said the job was too much; and (2) the evidence that he was not transitioning
13

well into the supervisory role, as reflected in negative reactions to coaching
and his combative interactions with staff.
75. Adgerson credibly testified that at the time of his decision he had no
awareness of any issues related to race, or any opposition to or complaint of
race discrimination by Saunders. He also noted that the skin-rubbing
incident outlined in Yoda's memorandum did not register with him as being
in the nature of a complaint of discrimination.
76. Adgerson had no direct communication with Yoda about Saunders at
any point during or after the process. His decision was entirely independent
and was based on the documentary record reviewed through five levels of
management and an independent civil rights office.
77. The failure-of-probation letter was signed by Deputy Director
Adgerson and delivered to Saunders on June 20, 2024. Saunders was then
returned to his bus operator position, effective that date. Resp. Ex. 1, at 2.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
78. DOAH has jurisdiction over the parties and subject matter of this
proceeding pursuant to sections 120.569, 120.57(1), and 760.11.
79. The Petitioner's case is based upon a violation of section 760.10(7)
prohibiting retaliation.
80. The Florida Civil Rights Act of 1992 ("FCRA") prohibits retaliation
against any person because that person has opposed a practice which is an
unlawful employment practice:
It is an unlawful employment practice for an
employer … to discriminate against any person
because that person has opposed any practice which
is an unlawful employment practice under this
section, or because that person has made a charge,
testified, assisted, or participated in any manner in
an investigation, proceeding, or hearing under this
section.
§ 760.10(7), Fla. Stat.
14

81. The FCRA is modeled after Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1965
("Title VII"), the federal antidiscrimination law. As a result, case law
interpreting Title VII is applicable to proceedings under the FCRA. Palm
Beach Cty. Sch. Bd. v. Wright, 217 So. 3d 163, 165 (Fla. 4th DCA 2017)
(en banc).
82. To arrive at the proper disposition of this case, the undersigned must
consider the elements of a retaliation claim under chapter 760.
83. Under the law, to establish a claim of retaliation, Saunders
must prove three things: (1) that he "engaged in a statutorily protected
activity," (2) that he "suffered an adverse action," and (3) that "the adverse
action was causally related to the protected activity." Gogel v. Kia Motors
Mfg. of Ga., Inc., 967 F.3d 1121, 1134 (11th Cir. 2020) (en banc).
84. The burden of proof is on Saunders to establish each element by a
preponderance of the evidence, and that unlawful retaliation occurred.
McAlpin v. Sneads, 61 F.4th 916, 927 (11th Cir. 2023).
85. Florida courts follow the same analysis for a retaliation claim.
See Buade v. Terra Grp., LLC, 259 So. 3d 219, 222 (Fla. 3d DCA 2018);
Carter v. Health Mgmt. Assocs., 989 So. 2d 1258, 1263 (Fla. 2d DCA 2008).2
86. Recently, in Kiernan v. ReviveMD305, 412 So. 3d 156 (Fla. 3rd DCA
2025), the Florida Third District Court of Appeals elaborated on additional
considerations in a retaliation case, and added:
"Opposing sexual harassment by reporting it to an
employer may qualify as statutorily protected
activity, see Vill. of Tequesta v. Luscavich, 240 So.
3d 733 (Fla. 4th DCA 2018), but a plaintiff-employee
must show that she "had a good faith, reasonable
belief that the employer was engaged in unlawful
employment practices." Hunsaker v. Found.
Partners Grp., LLC, No. 6:18-cv-1996-Orl-22DCI,
2020 WL 10355118 at *10 (M.D. Fla. 2020). "The
opposition must be directed at an unlawful
employment practice of an employer, not an act of
2 The parties agree that these are the elements to prove a claim of retaliation by Saunders.
15

discrimination by a private individual." Little v.
United Techs., 103 F. 3d 956, 959 (11th Cir. 1997)
(citation omitted).
In addition, the "plaintiff must show both that: (1)
she subjectively believed her employer engaged in
an unlawful practice, and (2) that this belief 'was
objectively reasonable in light of the facts and record
presented.'" Small v. City of Hollywood, 661
F.Supp.3d 1187, 1202-03 (S.D. Fla. 2023) (noting
"complaints about single instances of 'uncalled for,
ugly, racists statements' are not the kind of activity
protected by Title VII." (citation omitted)) (emphasis
added).
87. With this legal background in mind, and as more fully explained
below, the undersigned concludes that Saunders marginally proved the first
element ("he engaged in a statutorily protected activity"), satisfied the second
element ("he suffered an adverse action"), but Saunders failed in his proof
regarding the third element ("the adverse action was causally related to the
protected activity").
88. Whether Saunders had an honest or good faith belief that the County
discriminated against him or other employees is a factual question and, like
all matters of credibility, is solely for the factfinder to assess and determine.
See United States v. Grushko, 50 F.4th 1, 11 (11th Cir. 2022). The factfinder
may credit all, some, or none of a witness's testimony. AM Grand Court
Lakes, LLC v. Rockhill Ins. Co., 68 F.4th 1354, 1363-64 (11th Cir. 2023).
89. "The objective reasonableness of an employee's belief that [his]
employer has engaged in an unlawful employment practice must be
measured against existing substantive law." Clover v. Total Sys. Servs., Inc.,
176 F.3d 1346, 1351 (11th Cir. 1999). In this instance, Saunders would have
an objectively reasonable belief if a reasonable person would, under the
circumstances, believe that the County retaliated against him because of his
complaints or opposition to racial discrimination in his workplace.
16

First Element–Saunders Proved that He Engaged in Protected Activity
90. In this case, Saunders asserted two primary forms of protected
activity: (1) statements he made during a phone call with Yoda on April 18,
2024, about Yoda's alleged history of treating black employees poorly; and
(2) a skin-rubbing gesture during a subsequent meeting.
91. In a phone call with Yoda, Saunders claims that he complained, or
raised the point, that Yoda had a history of treating black employees poorly.
The undersigned credits this testimony by Saunders.
92. This, of course, was only an accusation, but it was premised on
Saunders's observations and his opinion of his treatment in the workplace
over time. It also took into account his knowledge regarding the history of
other black employees' reporting complaints of racial discrimination to FCHR
(Graham and Ferguson).
93. While these other complaints may have gone "unfounded," they
provided, at least, a basis for Saunders to believe that racial discrimination
was going on in his workplace. That, together with his own perceived
treatment, gave him a reasonable belief that discrimination existed.
94. The undersigned stresses that there is no independent finding being
made that racial discrimination was taking place–only that Saunders had a
subjective and reasonably objective belief that this environment existed.
95. The second allegation of protected activity is when Saunders rubbed
his forearm and said "I know what this is about" during the in-person
meeting with Yoda, Terrell, and the Union Representative Charles.
96. All three acknowledged during the hearing that they saw Saunders
make the gesture. Yoda and Terrell also testified that they knew, by the
gesture, that Saunders was pointing out he felt there was racial hostility in
the workplace.
17

97. The question is whether, in context, this gesture communicated a
good faith, objectively reasonable belief by Saunders that the County was
engaged in an unlawful employment practice. The undersigned finds that it
did.
98. The gesture occurred during a heated confrontation with Yoda, while
Yoda was attempting to address performance issues.
99. Both Yoda and Terrell reasonably understood this gesture was
Saunders's way of communicating or expressing to Yoda that he felt that
racial discrimination existed in the workplace. The point was clearly made by
Saunders. It may have been a crude way of doing so, but sometimes actions
do speak louder than words.
100. Nonetheless, it was his way of expressing his opposition to the
practice and culture that he believed existed at DTPW. Opposition to
unlawful practices can occur in a variety of ways and forms. Kiernan, 412
So. 3d at 156.
Second Element–Saunders Proved That Failure of Probation is an Adverse
Employment Action
101. The parties do not dispute that the failure of probation and return to
the bus operator position constitutes an adverse employment action within
the meaning of section 760.10(7). As a result, this second listed element for a
claim of retaliation under section 760.10 (7) was established.
Third Element–Saunders Failed to Prove a Casual Connection Between His
Protected Activity and the Above Employment Action
102. At this juncture in the case analysis, Saunders proof and case take a
fatal turn. Saunders failure to prove this final element involved a broad
range of evidentiary points and topics that scuttle or totally undermine
Saunders proof that a causal connection existed.
18

103. To start, direct evidence of the unreasonableness of Saunders's
argument that the County retaliated against him for his opposition, is found
in the comparator record of how other African Americans were treated
regarding TOS promotions.
104. For example, three black TOS trainees–Allen, Roberts, and Woods–
passed probation under the same superintendent during the same time
frame. Allen, who was in the same training class, testified that Yoda was a
stand-up manager and that race never affected their interactions.
105. Lead TOS Robledo, who worked alongside all four probationary
employees, confirmed that all three had some dispatch difficulties and still
passed, but Saunders "probably had the most errors."
106. Saunders cannot convincingly demonstrate retaliation where three
black colleagues in the same classification succeeded under the same
supervisor during the same time period, particularly where the independent
Office of Civil Rights and Labor Relations investigation found no evidence for
his retaliation claims. Further, his own union representative–who was
present at the April 18, 2024, meeting–did not witness racial animus by Yoda
nor did he file a grievance on Saunders's behalf.
107. Most significantly, the record is replete with numerous examples of
poor and deficient work performance by Saunders during his probationary
period. His refusal to accept more training, refusal to adapt and embrace the
multitasking required by the TOS job, and the insubordinate way he acted on
phone calls and in meetings with Yoda, were glaring. All provided a sound,
legitimate, and non-discriminatory basis to fail his probation.
108. At bottom, "Title VII's anti-retaliation provisions do not allow
employees who are already on thin ice to insulate themselves against
termination or discipline by preemptively making a discrimination
complaint." Alvarez v. Royal Atl. Devs., Inc., 610 F.3d 1253, 1270 (11th Cir.
2010).
19

109. Other evidence supports a conclusion that Saunders failed to
establish the third element–a causal connection between his protected
activity and the adverse employment action.
110. To establish a causal connection that an employee suffered an
adverse employment action "because of" his protected activity, courts usually
"look only to the conduct of the decisionmaker–the party with the 'power to
actually [affect] the employee's [status].'" Lewis v. City of Union City, 934
F.3d 1169, 1196 (11th Cir. 2019) (en banc) (Tjoflat, J., concurring in part and
dissenting in part) (quoting Stimpson v. City of Tuscaloosa, 186 F.3d 1328,
1331 (11th Cir. 1999)).
111. In Saunders's case, the final decisionmaker was Deputy Director
Adgerson. He testified unequivocally that he had no knowledge of any
protected activity–the phone call with Yoda or the skin-rubbing gesture–at
the time he made his decision to fail Saunders's probation.
112. In addition, Adgerson had no direct communication with Yoda about
Saunders at any point during or after the failure-of-probation process.
113. Adgerson was not motivated to retaliate since he had no
knowledge of the two instances of Saunders's opposition.
114. While the cat's paw theory was not advanced by Petitioner in his
proposed recommended order, it is briefly addressed and dismissed as
inapplicable to this case. The cat's paw theory derives from a fable conceived
by Aesop and injected into United States employment discrimination law by
Judge Posner in 1990. See Staub v. Proctor Hosp., 562 U.S. 411, 422 n.1
(2011).
115. Under the cat's paw theory, the animus of a biased supervisor who
reports to the decisionmaker can be imputed to the decisionmaker. Petitioner
must prove that: (1) the reporting supervisor acted with retaliatory animus;
(2) the supervisor intended to cause an adverse employment action; and
(3) the supervisor's biased act was the but-for cause of the ultimate adverse
action. See Staub, 562 U.S. at 422.
20

116. In general terms, the cat's paw theory seeks to hold an employer
liable for the animus of a supervisor who was not charged with making the
ultimate adverse employment decision, but improperly influenced the final
decision maker. Brnovich v. Democratic Nat'l Comm., 594 U.S. 647, 689
(2021).
117. However, the theory is not available in retaliation cases under Title
VII or the FCRA.
118. "Title VII retaliation claims require proof that the desire to retaliate
was the but-for cause of the challenged employment action." Univ. of Tex. Sw.
Med. Ctr. v. Nassar, 570 U.S. 338, 352 (2013). "In other words, a plaintiff
must prove that had [he] not engaged in the protected conduct," he would not
have suffered the adverse employment action. Gogel, 967 F.3d at 1135 (11th
Cir. 2020) (en banc).
119. More to the point, "[a] 'but-for' cause requires a closer link than mere
proximate causation; it requires that the proscribed animus have a
determinative influence on the employer's adverse decision." Sims v. MVM,
Inc., 704 F.3d 1327, 1335–36 (11th Cir. 2013).
120. Because Title VII retaliation claims require a "but-for" link between
the retaliatory animus and the adverse employment action, as opposed to
showing that the animus was merely a motivating factor in the decision, the
cat's paw theory "does not fit" Title VII retaliation claims. Mosley v. Preston
Cycles W., LLC, No. 21-13527, 2024 WL 2873720, at *5–6 (11th Cir. June 7,
2024) (citing Sims, 704 F.3d at 1336); see also Duncan v. Ala., 734 F. App'x
637, 640 (11th Cir. 2018) (cat's paw "is inappropriate when the statute
requires but-for causation").
121. The same limitation is true in Florida under chapter 760.10(7). See
Palm Beach Cnty. Sch. Bd. v. Wright, 217 So. 3d 163 (Fla. 4th DCA 2017) (en
banc) (The cat's paw theory does not apply to a FCRA retaliation case since it
applies a "but-for" causation standard.).
21

122. Ultimately, the undersigned was convinced that Saunders's failure of
probation as a TOS was not caused by or related to his opposition to Yoda
about his treatment of other black employees.
123. Rather, he failed probation because Yoda and other management
personnel reasonably concluded that his work performance, attitude, and
capabilities were not up to the standards expected for a TOS at DTPW.
124. In sum, the undersigned finds that Saunders has failed to prove by
a preponderance of the evidence that his protected activity was the but-for
cause of the failure of his probation. He has introduced no evidence from
which the undersigned could conclude that, absent the protected activity, the
failure of probation would not have occurred.
125. Based on the foregoing, the undersigned concludes that Petitioner
has failed to carry his burden to establish that Respondent, through its
employees, engaged in conduct that constituted retaliation against Petitioner,
in violation of section 760.10(7).
RECOMMENDATION
Based on the foregoing Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, it is
RECOMMENDED that the Florida Commission on Human Relations issue
a final order dismissing the Petition for Relief finding that Miami-Dade
County did not commit an unlawful employment practice in violation of
section 760.10(7).
